# Data Organisation

Among the six stock indices,S&P500 and CAC40 were selected to construct
an equally-weighted portfolio.We used the weekly closing price from 1
January 2000 to 31 December 2025. The data were combined and saved as a
CSV file named “S&P500_CAC40.csv”.na.omit() was used to make sure there
is no missing data.

```{r org, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE}
pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse, # Data handling
  VineCopula,
  fGarch,
  KScorrect,
  ADGofTest,
  fBasics,
  kableExtra
  )
# Read data
data <- read.csv("S&P500_CAC40.csv")
set.seed(1)

# Remove rows with missing values
clean_data <- na.omit(data)

# Format helper
format_pvalue <- function(p) {
  if (p < 0.001) return("p < 0.001")
  else return(paste("p =", round(p, 3)))
}
```

## Log-Return Plots

Now we start to construct appropriate time series models. The figure
below demonstrates log-return plots for both stocks. We can clearly
observe patterns of volatility clustering from the plots, that is,
periods of high volatility followed by high volatility, low volatility
followed by low volatility.

Both S&P500 and CAC40 indexes demonstrate extremely high volatility
between 2008 and 2009, coinciding perfectly with the Global Financial
Crisis. Similarly, both demonstrate high volatility in 2020 because of
the outbreak of COVID-19. By contrast, during the period 2004-2007,
2013-2019, the market shows low, gentle volatility. The CAC40 displays a
relatively more obvious volatility pattern, but overall, both CAC40 and
S&P500 show high similarity and synchronisation.This volatility
clustering phenomenon suggests possible autocorrelation in volatility.

```{r log_ret,echo=TRUE, fig.pos="H", fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
# Compute weekly log-returns
SP500_log_ret <- diff(log(clean_data$S.P500))
CAC40_log_ret <- diff(log(clean_data$CAC40))

# Calculate the variance-covariance matrix of log-returns
log_ret_cov <- cov(data.frame(SP500_log_ret, CAC40_log_ret))

#Create vector of portfolio weights, given they are equally-weighted
weight <- matrix(c(0.5,0.5), nrow = 1)

#Calculate portfolio variance
portfolio_var <- weight %*% log_ret_cov %*% t(weight)

#Create vector of expected log-returns
mean <- matrix(c(mean(SP500_log_ret), mean(CAC40_log_ret)), nrow = 1)

#Calculate expected log-return
portfolio_mean <- weight %*% t(mean)

#Calculate 95% and 99% VaR
VaR_95 <- qnorm(0.95) * sqrt(portfolio_var) - portfolio_mean
VaR_99 <- qnorm(0.99) * sqrt(portfolio_var) - portfolio_mean

#Plot log-return plots
dates <- as.Date(clean_data$Date[-1], format = "%Y/%m/%d")
returns_data <- data.frame(
  dates = dates,
  SP500 = SP500_log_ret,
  CAC40 = CAC40_log_ret
)

par(mfrow = c(2,1), oma = c(3,0,0,0))

plot(returns_data$dates, returns_data$SP500, type="l", xlab = "Time (year)", 
     ylab = "Log Returns", xlim = range(returns_data$dates), 
     ylim = c(-0.21,0.12), yaxt = "n", main="S&P500", col = "blue")
years_to_show = seq(2000, 2025, by = 5)
year_dates = as.Date(paste0(years_to_show, "/01/01"))
axis(1, at = year_dates, labels = years_to_show)
axis(2, at = seq(-0.20, 0.12, by = 0.15))

plot(returns_data$dates, returns_data$CAC40, type="l", xlab = "Time (year)",
     ylab = "Log Returns", xlim = range(returns_data$dates), yaxt = "n",
     main="CAC40", col = "darkgreen")
axis(1, at = year_dates, labels = years_to_show)
axis(2, at = seq(-0.25, 0.15, by = 0.15))
mtext("Figure 1: Traceplots of log-returns for two stock indices", 
      outer = TRUE, side = 1, line = 1)

```

# Constructing The Models

## **Box-Jenkins Identification**

To understand our data, we begin by assessing log-returns data against
the assumption of normality to aid later model selection.

```{r test1, echo=TRUE}
# JB test
SP500.jbt = format_pvalue(jarqueberaTest(SP500_log_ret)@test$p.value)
CAC40.jbt = format_pvalue(jarqueberaTest(CAC40_log_ret)@test$p.value)

# Skewness
SP500.Skew = skewness(SP500_log_ret) # -1.080232
CAC40.Skew = skewness(CAC40_log_ret) # -0.8701489

# Kurtosis
SP500.K = kurtosis(SP500_log_ret) # 7.074874
CAC40.K = kurtosis(CAC40_log_ret) # 7.847156

# DT Tables
initialTests = tibble(
  "Index" = c("S&P500", "CAC40"),
  "Jarque-Bera Test" = c(SP500.jbt, CAC40.jbt),
  "Skewness" = c(round(SP500.Skew, 2), round(CAC40.Skew, 2)),
  "Kurtosis" = c(round(SP500.K, 2), round(CAC40.K, 2))
)

## Output Table
kable(initialTests, 
      caption = "Initial Data Overview",
      booktabs = TRUE,
      row.names = FALSE,
      align = c("l","c","c","c")) %>%
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("hold_position"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    font_size = 9
  ) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = FALSE)%>%
  row_spec(0, 
           extra_css = "border-top: 1.5px solid black; border-bottom: 1.5px solid black;",
           bold = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(nrow(initialTests), 
           extra_css = "border-bottom: 1.5px solid black;") %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = FALSE)
```

Table 1 reveals that for each model normality is rejected through
significant Jarque-Bera tests at the 1% significant level, and strong
negative skewness, indicating heavier left tails than under normality.
These findings motivate the use of a heavy-tailed conditional
distribution in subsequent modelling. Following this, we take a
Box-Jenkin's approach to identify the order and volatility structures of
each indices we produce three diagnostic plots. The following
interpretations summarise our findings.

```{r acf, echo=TRUE, fig.align='center', fig.height=6, fig.width=4.5, out.width="100%"}
par(mfrow=c(3,2), oma = c(3,0,0,0), mar = c(3, 4, 1.5, 1))

acf(SP500_log_ret, col="blue", lwd=2, main="", xlab="", ylab="")
title(main="S&P500: ACF of Log-Returns", cex.main=0.8, cex.lab=0.7,
      xlab="Lag (Weeks)", ylab="Autocorrelation")
    
acf(CAC40_log_ret, col="green", lwd=2, main="", xlab="", ylab="")
title(main="CAC40: ACF of Log-Returns", cex.main=0.8, cex.lab=0.7,
      xlab="Lag (Weeks)", ylab="Autocorrelation")
acf(SP500_log_ret^2, col="blue", lwd=2, main="", xlab="", ylab="")
title(main="S&P500: ACF of Squared Log-Returns", cex.main=0.8, cex.lab=0.7,
      xlab="Lag (Weeks)", ylab="Autocorrelation")

acf(CAC40_log_ret^2, col="green", lwd=2, main="", xlab="", ylab="")
title(main="CAC40: ACF of Squared Log-Returns", cex.main=0.8, cex.lab=0.7,
      xlab="Lag (Weeks)", ylab="Autocorrelation")

pacf(SP500_log_ret, col="red", lwd=2, main="", xlab="", ylab="")
title(main="S&P500: PACF of Log-Returns", cex.main=0.8, cex.lab=0.8,
      xlab="Lag (Weeks)", ylab="Partial Autocorrelation")

pacf(CAC40_log_ret, col="purple", lwd=2, main="", xlab="", ylab="")
title(main="CAC40: PACF of Log-Returns", cex.main=0.8, cex.lab=0.7,
      xlab="Lag (Weeks)", ylab="Partial Autocorrelation")

mtext("Figure 2: ACF and PACF plots of log-returns and sqrt log-returns for 2 stock indices", 
      outer = TRUE, side = 1, line = 1, cex = 0.6)
```
\newpage
**ACF of Log-returns for S&P500 and CAC40**

For both indices, autocorrelations are consistently contained within the
95% confidence intervals. For S&P500, mild spikes occur around lags 2,
9, 15, and 29, for CAC40, mild spikes occur around lags 2, 8, 14, 15,
and 22. Due to the large number of observations in our data, and the
mild nature of these breaches, we feel there is insufficient evidence to
suggest true dependence, these lags likely exceed the bands by chance
due to variability within our sample.

**ACF of Squared Log-returns for S&P500 and CAC40**

We use ACF of squared log-returns to assess whether an ARCH/GARCH model
is required, as suggested by volatility clustering. Each index reflects
slow, geometric decays indicataing conditional heteroskedasticity
through persistence in autocorrelation. This provides sufficient
evidence for use of GARCH(1,1) within our model, as commonly used with
financial returns data.

**PACF of Log-returns for S&P500 and CAC40**

For both indices partial autocorrelation cuts off close to zero
following lag 1. Several moderate breaches of the 95% confidence bands
are found for both indices log-returns (e.g., lag 29 for S&P500 and lag
31 for CAC40) , which we attribute to sample variability, given our
large sample size (N=1,358), as opposed to true AR(29) and AR(31)
models. Given lag 2 of S&P500 does not strongly breach the confidence
bands, we proceed with an AR(1) model, including GARCH(1,1) effects.

## Assessing Model Fit

To confirm conditional distributions for each model, we compare
AR(1)+GARCH(1,1) models for both S&P500 and CAC40 under 4 candidate
distributions; normal distributions are excluded due to earlier
rejection of normality. Models are compared across AIC and BIC,
conditional on Ljung-Box test findings.

```{r func1, echo=TRUE}
whichConditionalFit = function(df, myCap) {
  
  myCap = gsub("&", "\\\\&", myCap) # Formating caption in Knit
  
  fitOne = function(ar.order) {
    results = data.frame(); i = 1 # Initialise loop + table
    formula = as.formula(paste0("~arma(1,0)+garch(1,1)")) # AR(1)GARCH(1,1) formula
    models = list(
      std   = garchFit(formula=formula, data=df, trace=F, cond.dist="std"), # Student-t
      sstd  = garchFit(formula=formula, data=df, trace=F, cond.dist="sstd"), # Skewed Student-t
      sged  = garchFit(formula=formula, data=df, trace=F, cond.dist="sged"), # Skewed GED
      ged   = garchFit(formula=formula, data=df, trace=F, cond.dist="ged") # GED
    )
    model_names = c("Student-t", "Skew Student-t", "Skew GED", "GED") # Match with table
    
    for (i in seq_along(models)) { # Loop for all
        model = models[[i]]
        res        = residuals(model, standardize=TRUE)
        lb_res     = Box.test(res,   lag=10, type="Ljung-Box", fitdf=1)
        lb_res_sq  = Box.test(res^2, lag=10, type="Ljung-Box", fitdf=0)
        results = rbind(results, data.frame(
          "Model" = model_names[i],
          "AIC" = round(model@fit$ics["AIC"], 2),
          "BIC" = round(model@fit$ics["BIC"], 2),
          `Ljung-Box` = round(lb_res$p.value, 2)
        ))
    }
    results
  }
  
  combined = fitOne(1)
  
  # Formatting
  
  kable(combined,
        caption = myCap,
        booktabs = TRUE,
        row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Model", "AIC", "BIC", "Ljung-Box"),
        align = c("l", rep("c", 3))) %>%
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9) %>%
    add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "AR(1)-GARCH(1,1)" = 3)) %>%
    row_spec(0, extra_css = "border-top: 1.5px solid black;") %>%
    row_spec(nrow(combined),
             extra_css = "border-bottom: 1.5px solid black;")
}
```

```{r cd1, echo=TRUE}
whichConditionalFit(SP500_log_ret, 'Selecting Conditional Distributions for SP500')
whichConditionalFit(CAC40_log_ret, "Selecting Conditional Distributions for CAC40")
```

Tables 2 and 3 compare conditional distributions across both indices.
Although Skewed Student-t shows marginally better BIC (-4.92 vs -4.89
for S&P500, -4.52 vs -4.51 for CAC40), we select Student-t based on
substantially stronger Ljung-Box results (0.66 vs 0.11, and 0.54 vs 0.18
respectively), indicating superior residual diagnostics - and better
overall fit. Below, we present our final models.

# **Final Model Selection**

```{r garch, echo=TRUE}
SP500.Model = garchFit(formula=~arma(1,0)+garch(1,1), data=SP500_log_ret, trace=F, cond.dist="std")
CAC40.Model = garchFit(formula=~arma(1,0)+garch(1,1), data=CAC40_log_ret, trace=F, cond.dist="std")
```

```{r func2, echo=TRUE}
getSummaryMetrics = function(model, title) {
  coef = model@fit$coef
  
  return(c(title, 
           round(coef["mu"], 2),
           round(coef["ar1"], 2),
           round(coef["alpha1"], 2),
           round(coef["beta1"], 2),
           round(coef["shape"], 2)))
}

compareModels = function(model1, name1, model2, name2, myCap) {
  myCap = gsub("&", "\\\\&", myCap)
  results = data.frame()
  
  r1 = getSummaryMetrics(model1, name1)
  r2 = getSummaryMetrics(model2, name2)
  
  results = rbind(results, r1, r2)
  
  colnames(results) = c("Model", "Weekly Mean", 
                        "AR(1) Coefficient", "Shock Sensitivity",
                        "Volatility Inertia", "Tail Shape")
  
  results = kable(results,
                  caption = myCap,
                  booktabs = TRUE,
                  row.names = FALSE,
                  align = c("l", rep("c", ncol(results) - 1))) %>%
    kable_styling(
      latex_options = c("hold_position"),
      full_width = FALSE,
      font_size = 9
    )
  return(results)
}
```

Both models share in fat tails and highly persistence-driven volatility
(both beta values \> 0.75). The S&P500 returns appear more shock-driven
(0.20 vs 0.09), indicating it reacts more strongly to immediate market
movements. While these models appear appropriate given PACF and
information criterion, we now formally evaluate whether our models
accurately characterise our data through PIT.

```{r compare, echo=TRUE}
compareModels(SP500.Model, "SP500", CAC40.Model, "CAC40", 
              myCap = "Comparing Student-t models for SP500 and CAC40 (2 d.p.)")
```

# Copula Modelling

## Probability Integral Transform

We fitted a copula model to find out the dependence structure between
the two stocks. To integrate the time series model with copula theory,
we adopt the conditional distribution (student-t distribution) from our
final models as the marginal distributions. To verify their adequacy, we
executed the following steps:

First, we extracted standardised residuals from our final models. As
shown in the upper part of our plots, the histogram of standardised
residuals perfectly matches the red fitted std density curves, showing
it is reasonable to choose student-t distribution.

Then we applied Probability Integral Transform (PIT) to those
standardised residuals. If the marginal models are correctly specified,
these transformed observations should strictly follow a standard uniform
distribution. As observed in the lower part of the plot, the histograms
are nearly uniform, showing that the marginal models are well-specified.

We implemented the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test and the Anderson-Darling
(AD) test on the PIT-transformed values. Both indices passed the KS test
(p\>0.05), indicating a good overall fit. Although the AD test showed
p\<0.05 due to its strict sensitivity to extreme tails, the uniform
pattern in the histograms in Figure 3 still supports our fitting. Based
on these results, we concluded that our chosen marginal models are
adequate, providing a solid foundation for the subsequent copula
modelling.

```{r pit, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
coef_SP500 <- SP500.Model@fit$coef
coef_CAC40 <- CAC40.Model@fit$coef

#PIT for S&P500
res1 <- residuals(SP500.Model, standardize=TRUE)
nu1 <- SP500.Model@fit$par["shape"]
u1 <- pstd(res1, mean=0, sd=1, nu=nu1)

# Implement Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
KStest1<-LcKS(u1, cdf = "punif")
invisible(KStest1$p.value)
# Implement Anderson-Darling test
ADtest1<-ad.test(u1, null="punif")
invisible(ADtest1$p.value)

#PIT for CAC40
res2 <- residuals(CAC40.Model, standardize=TRUE)
nu2 <- CAC40.Model@fit$par["shape"]
u2 <- pstd(res2, mean=0, sd=1, nu=nu2)

# Implement Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
KStest2<-LcKS(u2, cdf = "punif")
invisible(KStest2$p.value)
# Implement Anderson-Darling test
ADtest2<-ad.test(u2, null="punif")
invisible(ADtest2$p.value)
```

```{r plot, echo=TRUE, fig.height=9, fig.width=13, message=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(2,2), oma = c(3,0,0,0))

hist(res1, xlab = "S&P500 res", ylab = "density", 
     main = "Histogram of S&P500 Model Residuals", 
     ylim = c(0, max(c(hist(res1, plot=FALSE)$density, 0.5))), freq = FALSE)
curve(dstd(x, mean = 0, sd = 1, nu = nu1), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = "Student-t distribution", lty = 1, 
       col = "red", bty = "n")
hist(res2, xlab = "CAC40 res", ylab = "density", 
     main = "Histogram of CAC40 Model Residuals", 
     ylim = c(0, max(c(hist(res2, plot=FALSE)$density, 0.5))), freq = FALSE)
curve(dstd(x, mean = 0, sd = 1, nu = nu2), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = "Student-t distribution", lty = 1, col = "red")

hist(u1,xlab = "S&P500 u", 
     main = "Histogram of S&P500 Model Residuals after PIT", ylim = c(0,200))
hist(u2,xlab = "CAC40 u", 
     main = "Histogram of CAC40 Model Residuals after PIT", ylim = c(0,200))
mtext("Figure 3: Histogram of residual distribution before and after PIT for two stock indices", 
      outer = TRUE, side = 1, line = 2) 
```

## Copula-based Monte Carlo Simulation

In this step, we use `BiCopSelect` to fit copula model.The results
suggest us to use t copula based on the AIC criterion, with estimated
parameter par = 0.75, par2 = 6.11, tau = 0.54.

```{r copula1, echo=TRUE, fig.height=5, fig.width=10}
model <- BiCopSelect(u1, u2,familyset = NA, selectioncrit = "AIC", 
                     indeptest = TRUE, level = 0.05)
```

Then we generated 10000 simulated bivariate samples to create the
Simulated copula plot and compare it with the observed copula plot. We
also applied the Inverse Probability Integral Transform (IPIT) to
convert them into simulated standardised residuals. As shown in Figure
4, both copula plots show a clear lower-tail dependence, which suggests
that the simulated copula captures the key characteristics of the
dependence structure well. This indicates that large negative returns in
these two stocks happen together.

```{r copula2, echo=TRUE, fig.height=5, fig.width=10}
#set the length of the simulated bivariate sample
N <- 10000

# Should we consider using this for N?
# N = nrow(clean_data)

set.seed(1234)
u_sim <- BiCopSim(N,family = 2,par = model$par,
                  par2 = model$par2)

# Apply the component-wise Inverse Probability Integral Transform 
# SP500_sim<-qsstd(u_sim [,1],nu=nu1,xi=coef_SP500["skew"])
# CAC40_sim<-qsstd(u_sim [,2],nu=nu2,xi=coef_CAC40["skew"])

## Use "qtsd" instead. 
# Mean = 0, SD = 1 
SP500_sim <- qstd(u_sim[,1], mean=0, sd=1, nu=nu1)
CAC40_sim <- qstd(u_sim[,2], mean=0, sd=1, nu=nu2)

par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar = c(2, 2.5, 4, 1), oma = c(3, 0, 0, 0))
#Plot the Observed copula
plot(u1, u2, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = adjustcolor("gray37", alpha.f=0.4), 
     xlab = "S&P500", ylab = "CAC40", main = "Observed copula")

#Plot the simulated copula
plot(u_sim[,1], u_sim[,2], pch = 16, cex = 0.5, 
     col=adjustcolor("gray37",alpha.f=0.4), xlab = "S&P500",
     ylab = "CAC40", main = "Simulated copula")
mtext("Figure 4: Plot of observed and simulated copula", outer = TRUE, side = 1, line = 2) 
```

## Re-introducing Time Series Effects

For more realistic prediction of future returns, we re-introduced time
series effects observed in our original data. Specifically, we extracted
relevant parameters ($\mu$, $ar_1$, $\omega$, $\alpha$, $\beta$) from
previously built AR and GARCH models. Then, we introduced the last
return and volatility from the dataset and updated forward conditional
volatility $\sigma$. Following that, we rebuilt the simulated log
returns using these real parameters.

```{r ts, echo=TRUE}
# Re-introduce autocorrelation and GARCH effects observed in data
# Extract coefficients for S&P500
omega_S <- coef_SP500["omega"]
alpha_S <- coef_SP500["alpha1"]
beta_S <- coef_SP500["beta1"]
mu_S <- coef_SP500["mu"]
ar1_S <- coef_SP500["ar1"]

# Extract coefficients for CAC40
omega_C <- coef_CAC40["omega"]
alpha_C <- coef_CAC40["alpha1"]
beta_C <- coef_CAC40["beta1"]
mu_C <- coef_CAC40["mu"]
ar1_C <- coef_CAC40["ar1"]

# Extract the last non-standardised residuals from the model u
u_last_SP500 <- tail(residuals(SP500.Model, standardize = FALSE), 1)
u_last_CAC40 <- tail(residuals(CAC40.Model, standardize = FALSE), 1)

# Extract the last estimated conditional standard deviation from the model
sigma_last_SP500 <- tail(SP500.Model@sigma.t, 1)
sigma_last_CAC40 <- tail(CAC40.Model@sigma.t, 1)

# Extract the last observed log-return
y_last_SP500 <- tail(SP500_log_ret, 1)
y_last_CAC40 <- tail(CAC40_log_ret, 1)

# Update the conditional variance
sigma_sim_SP500 <- sqrt(omega_S + alpha_S * u_last_SP500^2 + beta_S * sigma_last_SP500^2)
sigma_sim_CAC40 <- sqrt(omega_C + alpha_C * u_last_CAC40^2 + beta_C * sigma_last_CAC40^2)

# Reconstruct the simulated one-step-ahead return
yS_simulated <- mu_S + ar1_S * y_last_SP500 + sigma_sim_SP500 * SP500_sim
yC_simulated <- mu_C + ar1_C * y_last_CAC40 + sigma_sim_CAC40 * CAC40_sim
```

## Plotting Original vs Simulated Log-returns

To test the validity of our simulation, we compared simulated log
returns with original log returns using Figure 5 below. We could easily
observe the strong overlap of simulated data (grey points) with original
data (red points) both in the central area and the tails. This suggests
that our model successfully reflects the joint distribution properties
of S&P500 and CAC40 in the real financial market.

```{r comp, echo=TRUE, fig.height=4, fig.width=7}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex = 0.8, oma = c(3, 0, 0, 0))

plot(SP500_log_ret, CAC40_log_ret, pch = 16, cex = 0.4, 
     col = adjustcolor("red", alpha.f = 0.4), xlab = "S&P500", ylab = "CAC40",
     main = "Distribution of Log-returns", 
     xlim = c(-0.1, 0.1), ylim = c(-0.12, 0.12)) 
points(yS_simulated, yC_simulated, pch = 16, cex = 0.3, 
       col = adjustcolor("gray50", alpha.f = 0.2))
legend("topleft", legend = c("Original data", "Simulated data"),
       col = c(adjustcolor("red", alpha.f = 0.6), adjustcolor("gray50", alpha.f = 0.6)), 
       pch = 16, pt.cex = 1.2, bty = "n")
mtext("Figure 5: Plot of original & simulated log-returns", outer = TRUE, side = 1, line = 2) 
```

## Compute Value-at-Risk

We estimate the 99% and 95% Value-at-Risk using Monte Carlo
simulation.The table below shows that 1-week VaR at 95% and 99%
confidence interval is 2.28% and 3.83%,respectively.With £1 million
invested, we are 95% confident that we will not lose more than £22,800
from investing over the next week and 99% confident that we will not
lose more than £38,300 from investing over the next week.

```{r var, echo=TRUE}
# Compute Value-at-Risk for the equally-weighted portfolio
port_sim <- log(1 + ((exp(yS_simulated) - 1) + (exp(yC_simulated) - 1)) * (1/2))

getVarVal = function(alpha) {
  value = round(-quantile(port_sim, 1 - as.numeric(alpha)),4)
}

var_sim = data.frame(
  "Alpha Level" = c("95%", "99%"),
  "Value-at-Risk" = c(getVarVal(0.95), getVarVal(0.99))
)

kable(var_sim, 
      caption = "Percentage Value-at-Risk for Balance Portfolio",
      booktabs = TRUE,
      row.names = FALSE,
      align = c("l", "c")) %>%
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("hold_position"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    font_size = 9
  ) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = FALSE)%>%
  row_spec(0,
           extra_css = "border-top: 1.5px solid black; 
           border-bottom: 1.5px solid black;",
           bold = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(nrow(var_sim),
           extra_css = "border-bottom: 1.5px solid black;") %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = FALSE)
```
